title: Full Name
Job Title
31 Questions that will identify your Sales DNA. Answer each question based on your instincts, there are no right or wrong answers
Q1. A buyer gives you a one-word answer after your opening question. Your instinct is to:
options: Ask another question immediately to keep momentum
Offer more context about your product to fill the gap
Acknowledge what they said and bridge to your next point
Mirror their last word or phrase back as a question
Label the feeling behind their short answer and hold silence

title: Q2. Mid-meeting, a buyer says: 'We've tried this before and it didn't work.' You:
options: Immediately explain why this time will be different
Apologise and offer a discount to rebuild goodwill
Ask them to tell you more about what happened
Reply: 'Didn't work?' and wait
Label: 'It sounds like that experience left you cautious about committing again.'

title: Q3. There is a 7-second silence after you ask a key discovery question. You:
options: Fill the silence with a clarifying follow-up question
Rephrase the question in case they didn't understand
Wait up to 5 seconds then gently prompt
Hold the silence, they are processing and will speak
Summarise what you've heard so far to give them something to react to

title: Q4. You call out a buyer's emotion incorrectly. They say 'I'm not worried,  I'm frustrated.' You:
options: Apologise and move on quickly
Defend your original read, they seem worried to you
Acknowledge the correction and ask them to tell you more
Use a follow-up statement: 'It sounds like I missed that, it's more frustration than worry.'
Pivot straight to a solution for frustration

title: Q5. A buyer says very little but their body language is tense. You prioritise:
options: Pushing through your agenda, they're just busy
Asking a direct question: 'Is everything okay?'
Slowing your pace and asking an open calibrated question
Narrating what you observe: 'It seems like there's a lot on your plate today.'
Acknowledging the tension and offering to reschedule

title: Q6. After a strong discovery session, a buyer goes cold and stops responding. You:
options: Send a 'just checking in' follow-up email
Call them and walk through your proposal again
Send a short email asking if priorities have shifted
Frame your response: 'It feels like your focus may have moved elsewhere, happy to pause if that helps.'
Wait two weeks before reaching out again

title: Q7. A client is venting about a difficult internal situation that has nothing to do with your proposal. You:
options: Listen politely then redirect to your agenda
Offer sympathy: 'I'm sorry to hear that'
Ask a question that connects their situation to your solution
Fully listen, then reflect back what you heard before moving on
Name what they're feeling and invite them to say more before pivoting

title: Q8. You sense a buyer is holding back, they're agreeable but not engaged. You:
options: Present more compelling data to re-engage them
Ask directly: 'Are you interested in moving forward?'
Ask an open question about their current priorities
Name what you notice: 'It seems like something hasn't quite landed yet.'
Give them space, push less, let them come to you

title: Q9. A major deal falls apart at the last minute due to internal politics you didn't see. Your immediate response is:
options: Review what data you could have presented differently
Analyse the relationship dynamics, who had influence you didn't map?
Follow up with the buyer to understand what changed
Accept it as part of the game and move to the next deal
Ask the buyer directly what the real reason was

title: Q10. A client gives you positive feedback to your face but doesn't return calls. You interpret this as:
options: They're genuinely interested but busy
They were being polite, the deal is probably dead
There's an internal obstacle they haven't told you about
A signal to send more proof points and case studies
An invitation to name the gap: 'It feels like something has shifted since we last spoke.'

title: Q11. In a group pitch, one stakeholder keeps interrupting with objections while others stay silent. You:
options: Address the loud objector head-on to neutralise the resistance
Pause and ask the quiet stakeholders for their perspective
Continue your pitch and handle objections at the end
Acknowledge the objector's concern then open to the room
Label the dynamic: 'It sounds like there are a few different perspectives in the room, let's surface them.'

title: Q12. A long-term client suddenly reduces their spend with no explanation. Your first move is:
options: Send a revised proposal with better pricing
Request a meeting to present new campaign options
Call and ask if something has changed on their end
Frame the situation: 'It seems like something has shifted, I'd rather understand it than guess.'
Speak to your manager before contacting the client

title: Q13. A Media Director says: 'Match this rate or the budget moves to your competitor.' You:
options: Match the rate to protect the relationship
Defend your rate card with audience and reach data
Acknowledge the pressure and ask what outcome they're optimising for
Label the pressure: 'It sounds like you're under internal pressure to reduce spend, what would success look like for you in this decision?'
Ask for time to consult your manager before responding

title: Q14. A buyer says 'We don't have budget' and then goes silent. You:
options: Immediately offer a lower-cost option
Ask when their budget cycle resets
Mirror: 'Don't have budget?' and hold silence
Ask what the budget situation looked like before this conversation
Summarise the ROI case to justify the spend

title: Q15. Mid-pitch, a senior stakeholder says 'I've heard all this before.' You:
options: Fast-forward to your most compelling slide
Acknowledge it: 'Fair, what would make this conversation worth your time?'
Defend your approach as different from competitors
Ask what they heard before that didn't land
Wrap up quickly and follow up with a tailored proposal

title: Q16. An agency contact says: 'Your competitor is offering CPC guarantees and post-click attribution. Can you match it?' You:
options: Commit to matching it, close the deal first, sort it out later
Explain why CPC guarantees are often misleading metrics
Acknowledge the ask: 'It sounds like attribution visibility is the real driver here, is that right?'
Ask what they would do with the attribution data
Offer a performance bonus structure as a compromise

title: Q17. You've used the phrase 'I completely understand' three times in a difficult meeting. You:
options: Don't notice, it's a natural empathy signal
Notice but it's better than silence
Recognise it's a filler, you need to ask a better question instead
Stop using it and replace it with a calibrated question
Use it once more, then pivot to closing

title: Q18. A client says 'The last campaign didn't move the needle, we need guarantees to proceed.' You:
options: Promise results to close the deal
Ask what 'moving the needle' means to them specifically
Present a new campaign structure with stronger targeting
Acknowledge: 'It sounds like the previous investment left you needing more certainty before committing again.'
Share a third-party case study showing comparable results

title: Q19. You have 2 minutes to introduce your solution in a first meeting. You start with:
options: Your company's reach and audience data
Your product's unique features versus competitors
A question about their biggest current challenge
A brief story about a client in a similar situation, time is of the essence
A specific client story using location, emotion, and a direct quote

title: Q20. A sceptical CMO asks 'Why should I choose you over your competitor?' You respond with:
options: A comparison of reach, CPM, and audience data
Your product's unique features versus competitors
A client success story with a specific outcome
You paint a picture: the client's situation before, what shifted, and you finish with their exact words
A question back: 'What would success look like for you in this space?'

title: Q21. You want to make a campaign result memorable in a presentation. You present it as:
options: 'We reached 450,000 people in the metro area'
'We filled ANZ Stadium five times over in a single breakfast shift'
'Our campaign delivered a 28% lift in sales'
'Our results exceeded industry benchmarks by 2.3x'
A before-and-after story ending with a client quote about the impact

title: Q22. Your media agency contact is taking your proposal into a boardroom without you. You ensure they can advocate for you by:
options: Including all the data they'll need in the deck
Briefing them on the top three product features
Giving them a clear ROI argument to use
Arming them with one short, vivid story they can retell confidently
Following up with a summary email after the meeting

title: Q23. A client is hesitating because the previous media partner 'let them down.' You address this by:
options: Highlighting your accountability processes and reporting
Offering a performance-based pricing model
Sharing a testimonial from a satisfied client
Telling a specific story of how you helped a client in a similar post-disappointment situation
Acknowledging their concern and moving to your product strengths

title: Q24. In your story, the client is the hero. This means:
options: You open with the campaign results and what your solution delivered
You focus on your team's strategic thinking and execution
You position the client's tension and relief as the emotional arc
You balance the narrative between the client's challenge and your company's response
You lead with the data and let the numbers speak for the work

title: Q25. When a client stops responding to your outreach, your gut says:
options: They're busy, keep following up
Something changed internally, I need to find out what
The deal is dead, move on
Acknowledge the silence directly without pressure, name what might be happening for them
Send one final message that creates a clear close or open. Force a response either way

title: Q26. You notice a five-second silence on a video call right after you've asked for the business. You:
options: Fill it immediately with reassurance
Repeat your ask in a different way
Hold the silence, you think they're processing
Ask if they have any final questions
Summarise your key points again

title: Q27. A client is calm and agreeable but you sense the deal isn't moving. You:
options: Take their positivity at face value
Ask about their decision-making timeline
Call out what you sense: 'It seems like something hasn't clicked yet, am I reading that right?'
Send a more detailed proposal to address any unstated concerns
Ask their media coordinator if there are any issues you should know about

title: Q28. The real reason a buyer says no is almost always:
options: Price — buyers are budget-constrained
Timing — the market isn't right
Risk — they fear looking bad if the campaign underperforms
Product — your offering doesn't fit their needs
Competition — a competitor made a better offer

title: Q29. When a buyer pushes back hard on your proposal, your first physical instinct is:
options: To defend your position, you believe in what you're selling
To apologise and offer a concession
To breathe, pause, and ask a question
To ask what specifically isn't working for them
To acknowledge the pushback and invite them to say more

title: Q30. The most important thing to understand about a buyer before you pitch is:
options: Their budget range
Their preferred media channels
Their KPIs and success metrics
What they personally fear will happen if this campaign fails
Their relationship with the previous media partner

title: Q31. Clients don't buy media plans. They buy:
options: Reach and frequency
Cost efficiency
Innovation and differentiation
Certainty that the campaign will deliver
Data-backed justification for their spend

title: EQ Identity
When a client is emotional my strength is.....
options: staying calm and not reacting
using their emotion as information to guide my next move
noticing the emotion before they've said anything
naming the emotion out loud, even when it's uncomfortable

title: Under pressure I........
options: stay logical and don't let feelings cloud my judgement
look for the emotional lever the other person hasn't used yet
watch and wait, reading the room before I act
call out what's really happening, even if it's awkward

title: After a difficult meeting I debrief by........
options: reviewing what logic/data I used
thinking about what emotional leverage I did or didn't use
replaying what I noticed, body language, silence, energy
thinking about whether I named the hard thing or avoided it
